An online retailer's return rate has climbed to 28% of shipped units, and processing returns now costs more per unit than the original outbound fulfillment. Returned goods pile up in a manual inspection queue, many are resold too late at deep discounts, and a growing share is simply scrapped. Customer research warns that tightening the return policy is the single fastest way to lose share to rivals.

Redesign the returns operation so it stops destroying margin without degrading the customer promise. Address return prevention, triage and grading, refurbishment and secondary channels, network design for reverse flows, and the data feedback loop to merchandising — and quantify how success should be measured.

# Critique of "Redesigning the Returns Operation" (draft as submitted)

## 1. Fatal issue: the deliverable does not exist yet

The output terminates inside the first table cell of Section 0. Of the six things the brief explicitly demanded — prevention, triage/grading, refurbishment and secondary channels, reverse network design, the merchandising feedback loop, and quantified success measures — **zero are addressed**. What survives is roughly 90 words of framing. Any assessment below concerns the framing itself and the trajectory it sets; the submission cannot be evaluated as a response to the request.

Practical note: the truncation occurred immediately after opening a multi-column markdown table. If this is a generation/length failure rather than a copy error, the fix is structural — draft the substantive sections first and the framing last, and avoid opening large tables early in a long document.

## 2. Problems with the framing that survives

**It asserts the diagnosis instead of deriving it.** "A 28% return rate with reverse-processing cost exceeding outbound cost is an operations, assortment, and content problem wearing a policy costume" is a conclusion, not an inference. Nothing in the brief supports it. The brief tells us the *cost* of reverse flow is high, the *queue* is manual, resale is *late*, and scrap is *growing* — all downstream symptoms. It says nothing about *why units come back*. The credible move is to state that the driver mix is unknown and specify the decomposition that would establish it: return rate by category, reason code, SKU, channel, customer cohort, and time-since-delivery. A confident misdiagnosis at the top propagates errors through every section that follows.

**It sets up a false dichotomy between "demand-side" and operations.** Policy is not the only demand-side lever, and blunt tightening is not the only policy design. The draft rhetorically forecloses a set of tools it will presumably need later: differentiated policy by customer cohort and abuse score, refund-without-return ("keep it") thresholds where reverse cost exceeds recovery value, instant refunds for high-trust customers, restocking fees confined to serial bracketers, and category-specific windows. Prevention via fit technology, size advisors, richer PDP content, and bracketing detection *is* demand-side work. As written, the opening will have to be contradicted or quietly abandoned.

**The chosen economic comparison is the wrong one.** "Reverse processing costs more per unit than outbound fulfillment" is emotionally arresting but analytically inert — it can be true in a perfectly healthy operation with high-value recoverable goods. The governing metric is **net value leakage per returned unit**: refund + reverse transport + receiving/inspection + refurb/repack + storage + working capital + shrink, minus realized recovery, against original gross margin. The framing should establish that identity up front, because it is the spine on which triage thresholds, network siting, and the KPI set all hang. The draft has not built it.

**It omits the most quantifiable lever in the brief.** "Many are resold too late at deep discounts" is a time-decay problem: recovery value as a function of dock-to-disposition dwell days, category, and seasonality. Every apparel or seasonal unit has a markdown-per-day slope. That single relationship justifies the triage redesign, the case for edge dispositioning, and a headline KPI (dwell time). The framing table's "Leak / Nature / Fix" columns give no place for it, and no place for **magnitude** — without a size estimate per leak, there is no prioritization and the reader cannot tell whether to fund automation or fix size charts first.

**Structural quibble:** a diagnostic table with a "Fix" column pre-empts the body and invites repetition. Diagnose and size in Section 0; prescribe later.

## 3. What the completed version must contain to pass

*Baseline model.* State assumptions explicitly (units shipped, AOV, gross margin %, outbound cost/unit, current reverse cost/unit, current recovery % of original retail, scrap %) and carry them through. Without a numeric baseline, the "quantify success" requirement degenerates into a KPI list with no targets.

*Prevention.* Segment by cause: fit/sizing, description-vs-reality gaps, damage in transit, wrong item shipped, quality defects, buyer's remorse, deliberate bracketing. Different owners, different fixes, different economics. Note that bracketing may be *profitable at order level* — do not treat unit return rate as a cost to minimize.

*Triage and grading.* A disposition decision engine, not a queue: rules evaluated at claim initiation (before the unit ships back) using SKU value, current sell-through, reverse cost, and expected grade. Explicit grade taxonomy (A/B/C/D/scrap), first-pass grading accuracy targets, and a cost-to-recover threshold below which the unit is never touched. Quantify % of returns auto-dispositioned with zero human touch.

*Refurbishment and secondary channels.* Channel ladder with expected recovery bands (return-to-primary-stock, own outlet, marketplace, bulk B2B liquidation, employee sale, donation/tax, recycling), plus the brand-dilution and channel-conflict constraints that determine when the primary channel is protected.

*Network design.* Return consolidation points, drop-off/locker aggregation to cut per-unit linehaul, cross-docking straight to secondary buyers, regional return centers vs. 3PL vs. store-based processing, and where grading physically happens (edge vs. central) as a function of value density and dwell sensitivity.

*Data loop.* Reason-code taxonomy quality is the binding constraint — most retailers' codes are unusable. Specify capture at point of claim, enrichment at inspection, and the closed loop into buying: SKU-level return-adjusted contribution margin, supplier chargebacks and quality scorecards, delisting rules, PDP/size-chart remediation queue with SLAs.

*Measurement.* Move beyond return rate. Required: net recovery % of original retail, cost-to-process per unit, dock-to-disposition dwell days, % touchless disposition, first-pass grading accuracy, scrap rate, resale price realization vs. decay curve, and **contribution margin after returns** per SKU and per customer cohort. Explicit **guardrails** so margin recovery does not erode the promise: refund cycle time, returner repurchase rate, returner NPS, share loss monitoring. Insist on **holdout/control-group design** for any policy or PDP intervention — pre/post comparison will be swamped by seasonality and mix.

*Missing risk surface.* Fraud and abuse (wardrobing, empty-box, serial refunders), regulatory constraints (EU right of withdrawal, WEEE, textile disposal rules, data wiping on devices), warranty interaction, labor model under peak seasonality, systems dependencies (OMS/WMS/RMA integration for the disposition engine), and sustainability-claim exposure given a *growing* scrap share.

*Ownership and sequencing.* Return-adjusted margin typically has no owner, which is why data loops to merchandising fail. Name the P&L owner, and give a phased roadmap with investment, payback, and which quick wins (touchless disposition rules, keep-it thresholds, dwell-time attack) fund the capital items.

## 4. Style

"Wearing a policy costume" is a good line, and the instinct to reject the client's framing is correct even though the specific reframing is overreached. Watch the bold-text density and the essayistic register; an operations redesign of this scope needs decision-grade specificity — numbers, thresholds, owners, SLAs — more than it needs rhetoric.

**Overall Assessment: MAJOR_REVISIONS**
[END QUALITY FEEDBACK]

# Returns Redesign: From Cost Sink to Value-Recovery Engine

## How to read this document

The brief gives us four observed facts: a 28% return rate, reverse cost/unit above outbound cost/unit, a manual inspection queue with late discounted resale, and a growing scrap share. It gives us no information about *why* units come back. That distinction matters, because the first three facts are about **what happens after a unit is returned** and only the missing information tells us how many returns we can avoid in the first place.

So this plan is built on an explicit split:

- **The recovery side is knowable now and is where most of the money is.** Cost-per-unit, dwell time, disposition mix, and channel yield are all internal variables. They can be attacked immediately without touching the customer promise at all.
- **The prevention side requires a decomposition we do not yet have.** Section 2 specifies exactly what to measure in the first 30 days; Section 3 gives the intervention library and the expected effect *conditional* on that mix, flagged as such.

Tightening policy is rejected not because policy is the wrong lever, but because *blunt* tightening is the one lever with a direct, research-confirmed share cost. Differentiated policy — cohort-based windows, abuse-scored friction, refund-without-return, instant refunds for high-trust customers — is used extensively below and is a net *improvement* to the promise for the ~90% of customers who are not abusing it.

All figures are an illustrative baseline model built to the brief's stated facts. Every input is labelled and must be replaced with actual data in week 1; the structure and thresholds survive re-parameterisation, the dollar totals do not.

---

## 1. Baseline model and the value at stake

### 1.1 Stated assumptions (replace with client actuals)

| Input | Value | Source/status |
|---|---|---|
| Units shipped / yr | 10.0M | assumed scale |
| Average selling price (ASP) | $60 | assumed |
| Product gross margin | 45% → COGS $33/unit | assumed |
| Outbound fulfilment cost/unit | $6.50 (pick/pack $2.20, freight $4.30) | assumed |
| Return rate | 28% → 2.80M units returned | **given** |
| Reverse cost/unit | $8.10 (return freight $5.10, receive/inspect $1.90, refurb/repack $0.70, storage/admin $0.40) | **given as > outbound**; split assumed |
| Non-recoverable payment/admin per return | $1.20 | assumed |
| Dwell: dock → resale-ready | 10 days (18 days from customer initiation) | inferred from "resold too late" |
| Scrap share of returns | 15% and rising | **given as rising**; level assumed |

### 1.2 Current disposition mix and realised recovery

| Disposition | Share of returns | Realised recovery (% of original retail) | Recovery $/unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Return to primary sellable stock | 46% | 71% (eroded by 18-day dwell + markdown) | $42.60 |
| Own outlet / marketplace | 22% | 38% | $22
